# ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes

Kaustubh Kumar Affiliation: TCS Research, Pune, India
Affiliation: Indian Institue of Technology, Patna, India Correspondence
to: <2201mm14_kaustubh@iitp.ac.in>    Ashutosh Ranjan Affiliation: TCS
Research, Pune, India Correspondence to: <ashutosh.ranjan2@tcs.com>   
Vivek Srivastava Affiliation: TCS Research, Pune, India Correspondence
to: <srivastava.vivek2@tcs.com>    Blessin Varkey Affiliation: TCS
Research, Pune, India Correspondence to: <blessin.varkey@tcs.com>   
Shirish Karande Affiliation: TCS Research, Pune, India Correspondence

###### Abstract

Understanding how artworks are created requires reasoning about the
iterative decisions, material operations, and contextual influences that
shape artistic production. While recent generative AI systems can
synthesize artworks with high fidelity, they primarily model
distributions over finished artifacts rather than the creative processes
underlying their creation. In practice, artistic workflows are only
partially documented through fragmented sources such as archival
records, preparatory studies, correspondence, etc., making process-level
understanding difficult to formalize computationally. In this work, we
introduce ArtMine, a framework for discovering and formalizing artistic
processes from heterogeneous historical evidence. Our approach
synthesizes heterogeneous artwork evidence into a structured repository,
from which a Peircean abductive agent infers evidence-grounded
production steps. These steps are converted into a compositional graph
and rendering prompt, then optimized through self-reflection over
deviations between the generated and reference artworks. We provide a
preliminary proof-of-concept case study using open-domain historical
sources across multiple artists and artistic movements, demonstrating
that fragmented documentary evidence can support coherent,
interpretable, and auditable representations of artistic workflows. By
modeling creative processes rather than only final artifacts, our work
moves toward process-centered human-AI co-creativity systems that can
support artistic interpretation, creative education, reflective
collaboration, and computational studies of cultural production.

###### Keywords: 

Multi-Agent Systems, Abductive Reasoning, Human-AI Co-Creativity,
Process Learning, Generative AI, Computational Art History

## 1 Introduction

Recent progress in generative AI has been primarily driven by learning
distributions over completed artifacts such as images, text, music, and
video ([Brown et al., 2020](#bib.bib1); [Ho et al., 2020](#bib.bib2);
[Rombach et al., 2022](#bib.bib3)). These systems can reproduce the
stylistic and semantic properties of human-created works with remarkable
fidelity, but they largely model what creative works look like rather
than how they are made. The sequence of decisions, revisions, material
operations, and intermediate reasoning that shape creative practice
typically remains latent.

This limitation matters for human-AI co-creativity, where collaboration
often depends on intermediate processes rather than final outputs alone.
Artists iteratively sketch, refine, critique, and revise their work,
while current generative systems operate primarily through
prompt-to-artifact generation. At the same time, substantial evidence
about creative processes already exists outside of the artifact itself.
Artist correspondence, preparatory sketches, conservation reports,
provenance records, technical imaging, and scholarly critique
collectively form a fragmented but information-rich record of artistic
production. Human scholars routinely use such evidence to reconstruct
plausible production trajectories and understand stylistic evolution.
However, despite advances in research agents ([Nakano et al.,
2021](#bib.bib4); [Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib5); [Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib6)) and computational creativity ([Cohen,
1995](#bib.bib7); [Colton, 2012](#bib.bib8)), these documentary records
have rarely been treated as supervision to model creative processes.

In this work, we study artistic process discovery and formalization: the
task of inferring structured, auditable sequences of production steps
for artworks from heterogeneous historical evidence. The objective is to
recover plausible creative trajectories that explain how an artwork may
have been produced, while preserving explicit links between inferred
actions and their supporting sources. We frame this task as an abductive
inference under incomplete information ([Josephson and Josephson,
1996](#bib.bib44); [Peirce, 1997](#bib.bib10); [Kakas et al.,
1992](#bib.bib9)). Given an artwork and a heterogeneous corpus of
documentary evidence, the system incrementally constructs hypotheses
about the latent process that could plausibly have produced the work
while remaining consistent with the available historical and material
record.

![Refer to caption](2607.08331v1/71_ArtMine_Discovering_and_For.png)

Figure 1: ArtMine. Architecture diagram of our proposed framework for
discovering and formalizing artistic processes.

To address this task, we propose ArtMine, a framework that integrates
deep-research-based evidence construction, structured evidence
repository, Peircean abductive reasoning, and self-reflection-driven
policy updates for artistic process discovery. A deep-research agent
organizes open-domain evidence into a structured concept schema. An
abductive agent then uses this repository to infer process trajectories
under a Peircean policy linking observations, rules, and hypothesized
production actions. The inferred trajectory is rendered, compared with
the reference artwork using multi-reward feedback, and iteratively
improved through self-reflection-driven policy updates (see Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")).
Our case study demonstrates that heterogeneous historical evidence can
be organized into structured representations suitable for downstream
reasoning, and that abductive reconstruction can generate coherent and
auditable production trajectories grounded in those records. Our
contributions are threefold:

1.  1.  We introduce artistic process discovery and formalization as a
        computational problem for generative AI, shifting the focus from
        modeling completed artifacts to reconstructing creative processes
        from heterogeneous historical evidence.
2.  2.  We propose ArtMine an agentic framework that combines
        deep-research-based evidence construction, Peircean abductive
        reasoning, and se to reconstruct auditable creative trajectories
        from unstructured documentary and archival records.
3.  3.  We present a case study as proof-of-concept reconstructions
        demonstrating that open-domain documentary and evidence can support
        structured inference over creative processes.

## 2 Related Work

Recent research-agent systems extend retrieval-augmented generation with
iterative planning, tool use, reflection, and web interaction ([Lewis et
al., 2020](#bib.bib11); [Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib5); [Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib6); [Nakano et al., 2021](#bib.bib4)). These systems
demonstrate that language agents can gather and synthesize information
from heterogeneous online sources through multi-step reasoning and
interaction. Our work builds on this direction by using a Deep Research
agent to gather evidence from multiple sources, synthesize claims across
these sources, assign reliability tags to retrieved evidence, and
organize the resulting information into a structured evidence repository
for downstream abductive reasoning. Rather than treating retrieved
information as unstructured context for generation, the resulting
evidence is organized into structured representations that support
downstream reasoning about creative processes.

Role-conditioned and persona-conditioned language agents aim to maintain
behavioral or stylistic consistency during generation. Early work
represented personas through static textual profiles in dialogue systems
([Zhang et al., 2018b](#bib.bib13); [Mazaré et al., 2018](#bib.bib12)),
while more recent approaches study role-playing and
character-conditioned generation in large language models. ArtPeer
([Kumar et al.,](#bib.bib14) ) explores artist-centered persona
construction from art-historical sources, while CharacterGLM ([Zhou et
al., 2024](#bib.bib15)) studies character-consistent generation under
persona conditioning. In most of these systems, personas primarily
function as conditioning mechanisms for generating stylistically or
behaviorally consistent outputs. In contrast, our framework evaluates
discovered process trajectories through artwork-grounded policy
optimization, where rendered artwork are compared with reference
artworks and the resulting deviations drive self-reflection-based policy
updates.

Our work is also related to computational creativity and generative art
systems. Classical systems such as AARON ([Cohen, 1995](#bib.bib7)) and
The Painting Fool ([Colton, 2012](#bib.bib8)) generate artworks through
procedural rules and heuristic creative strategies. More recent
generative models such as DALL$`\cdot`$E 3 ([Betker et al.,
2023](#bib.bib16)), Stable Diffusion ([Rombach et al.,
2022](#bib.bib3)), and Jukebox ([Dhariwal et al., 2020](#bib.bib17))
learn distributions over artistic artifacts from large-scale multimodal
data. Agent-based simulations of social behavior and interaction ([Park
et al., 2023](#bib.bib18)) similarly model emergent behaviors through
multi-agent interaction. In contrast, our work focuses on discovering
historically grounded creative trajectories from documentary, archival,
technical, and art-historical evidence, and refining them through
artwork-grounded self-reflection rather than treating generation as a
one-shot artifact-production task. A detailed discussion of the related
works is presented in the Appendix
[A](#A1 "Appendix A Related Work ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes").

## 3 Method

### 3.1 Evidence Construction

Discovering how an artwork was made requires more than describing its
visible surface. The finished object shows the result, not the order of
actions, revisions, abandoned alternatives, or decisions that produced
it, and since different processes can yield similar effects, the object
alone does not determine its own history. Process discovery therefore
requires external knowledge: artist letters and preparatory studies
([Van Gogh, 2009](#bib.bib37)), imaging and pigment studies ([Zhao et
al., 2008](#bib.bib38); [Delaney et al., 2016](#bib.bib39)), museum and
auction records, and later scholarship. These sources constrain what is
plausible, as technical studies reveal hidden layers and materials,
correspondence records intent and working conditions, and preparatory
studies expose earlier states. But they differ in reliability: a
statement by the artist, a conservation report, and a speculative claim
cannot be treated alike, and once retrieved as plain text, these
differences are easily hidden. Since downstream reasoning depends on the
reliability of evidence ([Shi et al., 2023](#bib.bib40)), evidence
typing must occur while knowledge is gathered, not after it.

We construct the evidence repository $`\mathcal{M}_{\text{evidence}}`$
using a Deep Research agent that plays two roles. First, it retrieves
information about the artwork from open-domain sources, such as museum
collection records, conservation and technical reports, artist
correspondence, archival documents, exhibition catalogs, scholarly
articles, provenance records, etc. Second, it organizes that information
into a concept schema with 11 dimensions: metadata, historical context,
materials and technique, formal analysis, iconographic analysis,
documentary evidence, provenance, scientific analysis, interpretations,
cultural impact, and conflicts. This schema is designed to capture both
iconographic and technical aspects of an artwork. The iconographic
dimensions focus on visual content, symbolic meaning, and interpretation
([Panofsky, 2018](#bib.bib42)), while the technical dimensions record
materials, methods, condition, provenance, and scientific findings
([Hermens, 2012](#bib.bib43)). To support reasoning under uncertainty,
the repository also preserves disagreement between sources. When sources
offer conflicting claims, the agent does not collapse them into a single
reconciled statement; instead, it stores the competing positions in a
dedicated conflicts category. This allows the abductive solver to
compare alternative explanations while maintaining an explicit awareness
of uncertainty in the evidence.

Figure 2: Distribution of evidence sources across $`M_{evidence}`$,
counted as the number of times each source category is utilized across
all evidence assertions in our case study.

The evidence in the repository is tagged by how it was obtained: the
Deep Research agent assigns each piece of evidence a tag based on its
source and method of discovery, either direct_evidence,
indirect_evidence, interpretation, or speculative ([Howell and
Prevenier, 2001](#bib.bib41)). Here, direct_evidence refers to primary
sources, such as artist letters, archival records, museum entries,
conservation reports, etc. Indirect_evidence captures claims inferred
from contextual or secondary sources, including biographies, exhibition
histories, related artworks, or known workshop practices. Interpretation
denotes scholarly readings of meaning, symbolism, style, or intention,
while speculative marks low-certainty claims that lack strong
documentary or material support. These distinctions allow the abduction
agent to reason with graded reliability instead of treating all
retrieved claims as equally trustworthy. For example, a signed letter by
the artist and a speculative claim from popular writing then carry
different weight in reasoning, rather than being treated as equally
reliable.

The agent is also instructed not to invent missing information or merge
the interpretation with fact. As a result,
$`\mathcal{M}_{\text{evidence}}`$ is not a flat text summary but a
structured evidence base where each claim carries its source,
reliability, and uncertainty. An example
$`\mathcal{M}_{\text{evidence}}`$ for Mona Lisa is provided in the
Appendix
[B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Mona Lisa ‣ Appendix B Populated Memory ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes").

### 3.2 Abductive Process Discovery

The evidence repository gives a structured account of what is known
about an artwork but does not by itself explain how the artwork was
made. It contains claims about materials, visual features, documents,
provenance, and technical findings, but these claims must still be
turned into a process. We therefore use an abductive agent to move from
evidence to process. The goal is to infer a trajectory $`\tau`$ that
explains how a blank canvas could have been transformed into an artwork
consistent with the evidence in $`\mathcal{M}_{\text{evidence}}`$.

Abduction is appropriate for this setting because the process is not
observed directly. The agent observes the finished artwork and the
records around it, and tries to abduce which sequence of actions would
best explain them ([Josephson and Josephson, 1996](#bib.bib44);
[Kapitan, 1992](#bib.bib45); [Hoffman et al., 2020](#bib.bib46)). The
deduction is too strict for this task since no general rule entails the
making of a particular painting. Induction is also limited, since we do
not have a large set of comparable making processes from which to learn
a reliable pattern. Abduction, instead, reasons backwards from observed
evidence to a plausible explanation. Although recent work shows that
language models can perform abductive inference ([Bhagavatula et al.,
2019](#bib.bib22)), our setting requires the inference to remain
grounded in an external evidence repository.

#### 3.2.1 Policy Initialization

The abductive agent ($`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{abd}}`$) is initialized with
a policy $`\Pi_{i}=(R,\Sigma,C)`$ that governs how it reasons over the
evidence. The role $`R`$ asks $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{abd}}`$ to act as
an art-historical process reconstruction system. Following Peirce’s
account of abduction as inference to the best explanation ([Peirce,
1997](#bib.bib10)), the abductive protocol $`\Sigma`$ expresses each
step as a triplet: an observation of a feature of the work, a rule
stating that a process of type $`P`$ would produce that feature, and a
hypothesis that selects the concrete production action $`P`$ which,
under the stated rule, best explains the observed feature. Unlike the
original Peircean triplet, which leaves the inferred process
underspecified for downstream generation, $`\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{abd}}`$
extends $`\Sigma`$ by adding both an action and an evidence to each
inferred step. The action translates the abductive hypothesis into a
concrete production instruction that can be carried forward by later
modules, such as DAG construction and prompt generation. The evidence
then binds the observation of the step to a specific unit of the
repository and carries the reliability tag of the unit, so the action
remains traceable to its supporting source ([Howell and Prevenier,
2001](#bib.bib41)). The constraint set $`C`$ further requires the agent
to cite evidence, avoid unsupported claims, and remain close to the
production logic of the painting. The complete policy is provided in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Evidence Construction ‣ 3 Method ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")
and prompt for the agent is provided in the Appendix
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes").

Under this policy, the agent reconstructs an initial trajectory
$`\tau=(s_{1},\dots,s_{N})`$ in production order. It observes the
reference work and, at each step, emits an abductive quadruple grounded
in a repository unit and conditioned on the steps already committed.
Since the policy requires each abductive quadruple to include an
evidence key if no such key can be supplied, the step is treated as
unsupported and excluded from the trajectory. In this way, the
trajectory is grounded and provides an initial evidence-linked
explanation of how the artwork may have been made.

#### 3.2.2 Policy Learning

The process is abduced by the initial policy from
$`\mathcal{M}_{\text{evidence}}`$ alone and is never tested against the
way its choices look once drawn. The initial process is therefore
unverified, and it may misplace an element, misjudge a proportion, or
set the wrong palette.

Correcting the initial process requires rendering it as an image and
comparing the result with the reference artwork. Prior work on
self-evolving agents has shown that feedback from past trajectories can
improve an agent’s capabilities through policy optimization ([Zhang et
al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib63); [Yin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib65); [Kakade et al., 2026](#bib.bib64); [Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib66)). Motivated by this view, we formulate policy learning
as multi-reward-driven self-reflection, where reconstruction feedback is
used to update the abductive policy from ($`\Pi_{i}`$) to
($`\Pi_{i+1}`$). The abductive agent compares the rendered image with
the reference artwork, analyzes deviations in elements such as
composition, palette, position, and form, and reflects on the likely
causes of these errors. The resulting feedback is incorporated into the
policy for the next iteration, so that subsequent trajectories remain
consistent with both the evidence repository and the visual appearance
of the target artwork. The components of this loop are described below.

##### Compositional graph construction.

From $`\tau`$, the composition agent reads each step and extracts the
specification of the corresponding visual element, together with
attributes such as colour, size, position, and brushwork texture. For
example, a step such as “paint a seated central figure in muted earth
tones with softly folded hands in the lower foreground” is decomposed
into an element node for the sitter, attribute nodes for palette and
scale, and relational information specifying the position of the hands.
The agent then compiles the trajectory into a directed acyclic graph
(DAG) $`G`$, whose nodes are visual elements and whose edges connect
each element to the element it builds on.

Each edge in $`G`$ has two labels. The first label specifies the
relation between the child element and its parent, such as whether the
child refines, overlaps, sits over, or accents the parent. The second
label specifies the relative position of the child with respect to the
parent, for example, whether a hand appears in the lower foreground of
the sitter, or a bridge is placed in the distant background behind the
figure. The elements whose out-degree exceeds a predefined threshold are
selected as focal elements; that is, they are the visual elements on
which many other elements depend. These focal elements jointly anchor
the composition. Unlike a flat list of steps, the DAG preserves both the
partial order of making and the relational-spatial structure needed for
the artwork reconstruction prompt. The prompt for the composition agent
is provided in the Appendix
[D.4](#A4.SS4 "D.4 DAG Construction Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes").

##### Artwork reconstruction prompt.

The visual prompt agent composes the artwork reconstruction prompt from
$`G`$. It leads with the focal element, then places each remaining
element by its relative position to the element it builds on, carrying
the attributes from the attribute nodes. It drops artist and title
identifiers, so the generator works from the reconstructed appearance
rather than from a named work it already knows. A text-to-image model
renders the prompt in a generated image $`I`$. The prompt for the visual
prompt agent is provided in the Appendix
[D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 DAG to prompt construction ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes").

##### Multi-reward scoring.

We compare $`I`$ with the reference artwork $`I_{\mathrm{ref}}`$ along
three complementary rewards. The style reward (CSD ([Somepalli et al.,
2024](#bib.bib47))) measures agreement in brushwork, palette, and
surface character. The perceptual reward (LPIPS ([Zhang et al.,
2018a](#bib.bib48))), measures low-level texture and structural
agreement. The semantic reward (CLIP ([Radford et al.,
2021](#bib.bib49))) measures whether the depicted content matches the
reference.

##### Self-reflection and Policy updation.

The abduction agent closes the loop by working out why the rendering
falls short and what should change. It looks at the rendered and
reference artworks together, guided by the multi-reward vector and the
ordered actions that produced the image. Reading the rendering against
the reference artwork element by element, it notes where an element is
missing or where its colour, size, position, or shape has drifted, and
assesses the severity of each divergence. What it learns from this falls
into two categories. The first, the method-principles
$`\mathcal{C}_{g}`$, are generic to the art-creation process, such as
how to order layers or set a palette from the evidence, so they are
folded back into the policy $`\Pi_{i}`$ and carried forward to every
subsequent run.

The second category consists of artwork-specific corrections
$`\mathcal{C}_{a}`$, which capture adjustments required by the
particular target work, such as softening the sitter’s smile,
repositioning the folded hands in the lower foreground, refining the
atmospheric background, etc. Rather than being converted into general
rules, these corrections are stored in a per-work memory
$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{art}}`$. During the process discovery of the next
artwork, this memory is provided as a set of worked examples that the
agent may adapt when the new evidence supports a similar compositional
or material decision.

When the rendered artwork still exhibits substantial divergence from the
reference, the reflection $`r_{\Pi}`$ produced under the current policy
is used to revise the policy. The updated policy is formed as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \Pi_{i+1}=(R,\Sigma\cup\mathcal{C}_{g},C\cup\mathcal{C}_{a}),
       ```                                                            |     | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{C}_{g}`$ extends the abductive protocol $`\Sigma`$ with
reusable process-level principles, and $`\mathcal{C}_{a}`$ extends the
constraint set $`C`$ with artwork-specific corrections. Duplicate
entries are discarded. The loop then reruns under $`\Pi_{i+1}`$ and
continues as long as the rendered artwork improves. An example of an
updated policy is presented in the Figure
[4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.1 Evidence Construction ‣ 3 Method ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes").
The self-reflection loop stops when one of three conditions is met:
Acceptance, where the mismatch severity becomes small, and all rewards
stop changing meaningfully; No-progress, where the mean reward declines
for $`K`$ consecutive iterations; or Budget, where the iteration limit
is exhausted. Since a later update can sometimes lower a reward, the
system returns the best-scoring iteration rather than the last. This
state consists of the inferred trajectory $`\tau`$, the generated image
$`I`$, the reward vector $`s`$, and a termination label indicating
whether the loop ended by acceptance, no-progress, or budget exhaustion.

#### 3.2.3 Formalizing the learned policy via Cross-Artwork Transfer

ArtMine applies the policy learning loop across a sequence of canonical
artworks $`A_{1},\dots,A_{T}`$. The learned policy is carried forward,
so the method-principles $`\mathcal{C}_{g}`$ and artwork memory
$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{art}}`$ accumulate into a trained policy
$`\Pi^{\ast}`$.

After learning across the canonical sequence, ArtMine freezes the policy
$`\Pi^{\ast}`$ and applies it once to a new artwork, abducing and
rendering a trajectory with no further updates. Any gain must then come
from the inherited method-principles and artwork memory, so this setting
tests whether the policy transfers to a low-evidence regime.

ArtMine renders the discovered trajectory in three modes. Single-pass
renders the full trajectory in one pass, as during learning, yielding
one image from the complete prompt. Direct stage-wise splits the
trajectory into ordered stages, each combining one or more steps of the
$`\tau`$, and renders every stage independently from its partial DAG.
Guided stage-wise renders the stages in sequence, conditioning each on
the previous image so later stages layer over earlier ones. These three
modes let us assess how good the discovered process is and whether it
can be rendered step by step.

### 4.1 Experimental details

Evidence construction is performed with a Deep Research agent built on
MiroThinker 1.7 mini ([Team et al., 2025](#bib.bib50)). Given an artwork
and artist name, the agent retrieves open-domain evidence and organizes
it into the concepts schema described in
Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Evidence Construction ‣ 3 Method ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes").
The remaining reasoning components share the same backbone: the
abductive solver, composition agent, and visual prompt generation agent
all use Qwen2.5-VL. Image generation is performed with FLUX.1-dev.

![Refer to caption](2607.08331v1/gtg_both.png)

Figure 7: Direct and guided staged reconstruction for The Girl at the
Gate by George Clausen. The top panel shows direct stage-wise
generation, where each stage is generated independently. The bottom
panel shows guided stage-wise generation, where each stage is
conditioned on the previous generated stage, resulting in a more
coherent reconstruction trajectory.

We evaluate process discovery through artwork reconstruction. We compare
the generated artwork against the reference image along three
complementary axes. CSD measures stylistic similarity, especially
brushwork, palette, and surface character. LPIPS measures low-level
perceptual distance. CLIP measures semantic agreement between the
generated image and the reference content. We track the three scores
separately rather than collapsing them into a single scalar, because the
weakest axis identifies the main failure mode that reflection should
address in next iteration.

### 4.2 Dataset

Following ([Kumar et al.,](#bib.bib14) ), we use ten artworks sourced
from WikiArt, split into five canonical and five non-canonical works.
The canonical set comprises Impression, Sunrise, Café Terrace at Night,
Guernica, The Scream, and the Mona Lisa. The non-canonical set comprises
The Girl at the Gate by George Clausen, Horse and Cart by Georges
Seurat, Two Riders by a River by Edgar Degas, Cat and Canary by Will
Barnet, and A Walk at Dusk by Caspar David Friedrich.

We compare the ArtMine against a set of prompting strategies that share
its backbone and generator, but omit its policy learning.

[11](#A4.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ D.6 Self-Reflection Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes"))

$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{evidence}}`$ ablation. We run every strategy in
two settings. With $`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{evidence}}`$, the strategy
receives the structured evidence repository
$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{evidence}}`$ for the artwork, so its
reconstruction can be grounded in the documented materials, technique,
and iconography. Without $`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{evidence}}`$, the same
strategy receives only the reference image and must infer the process
from what it observes.

![Refer to caption](2607.08331v1/quali_example.png)

Figure 8: Qualitative comparison of reconstruction methods on a
canonical and a non-canonical artwork. Each row shows the reference

## 5 A Case Study

We illustrate the framework through artwork reconstruction on the
canonical and non-canonical works. The study is intended as a
proof-of-concept exploration of how abductive policy learning and
structured evidence synthesis support interpretable representations of
artistic process.

### 5.1 Structured Evidence Repository

$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{evidence}}`$ helps to discover production order.
$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{evidence}}`$ organizes art-historical information
as constraints on how the artwork could have been made. These
constraints give the abductive agent the evidence it reasons over to
recover a plausible order of production. For the Mona Lisa
(Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Mona Lisa ‣ Appendix B Populated Memory ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")),
evidence about the thin poplar panel grounds the support that must
precede all painting, and infrared findings recover the chair,
balusters, etc., the darkened surface hides. Technical evidence about
sfumato then grounds the later steps that model the mouth, eyes, hands,
and landscape. From these constraints, the agent infers the production
order, placing the support first and the sfumato modelling last,
grounded in documented technique rather than visual appearance.

Preserved conflicts guide the abduction agent.
$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{evidence}}`$ also reduces overconfident
reconstructions by preserving the reliability of each claim. Each item
is tagged by evidence type, so interpretive readings are not weighted
like museum or conservation records, and as
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Evidence Construction ‣ 3 Method ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")
shows, most support comes from those sources. Conflicts are kept rather
than resolved: for The Scream, $`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{evidence}}`$
records disagreement over the figure’s sex and dress, which prevents the
agent from committing to unsupported details and abduce an androgynous
figure. (Refer to Section
[B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 The Scream ‣ Appendix B Populated Memory ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")).

### 5.2 Abductive Process Discovery

Visuals alone cannot determine process. The abductive agent infers a
plausible artistic process from the evidence stored in
$`\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{evidence}}`$. For each observed feature, it tries
to hypothesise which operation naturally explains its presence. A visual
description of the Mona Lisa may note a seated woman, folded hands, a
dark costume, and a distant landscape, but not the process behind it.
The abduction agent bridges this gap by inferring the sequence of
artistic operations that could have produced the observed work.

Abduction bridges appearance and process. The
Appendix [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Mona Lisa ‣ Appendix C Process Synthesis Output ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")
synthesis output illustrates this for the support step. The observation
is a large, thin poplar panel, and the rule is that any support precedes
all paint. From these, the agent infers that Leonardo prepared the panel
first and adds panel preparation as the opening action. Infrared
evidence of a chair, balusters, and a balustrade works the same way. The
agent infers that the pose and loggia setting were planned early, and
adds an underdrawing action before any modelling.
Figure [6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4 Experimental setup. ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")
(b) shows these stages in order, from layout through dead colouring,
first modelling, upper layers, synthesis, and a final surface
adjustment. The same pattern holds beyond the Mona Lisa. In Café Terrace
at Night, the glowing terrace and blue-violet street become a plan to
organize the cafe, street, and sky first, then build the warm–cool
contrast through colour and brushwork (Refer to Sectionn
[C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Cafe Terrace at Night ‣ Appendix C Process Synthesis Output ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")).

### 5.3 Policy Optimization and Transfer to Non-Canonical Artworks

Learned policy tends to improve reconstruction. The base policy
$`\Pi_{0}`$ carries only the Peircean structure
(Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Evidence Construction ‣ 3 Method ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")),
which grounds an initial trajectory. Policy learning improves this
policy by comparing the rendered image generated using the initial
process with the reference. On the canonical works ArtMine outperforms
every prompting baseline, with better CSD, CLIP, and LPIPS
(Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Abductive Process Discovery ‣ 5 A Case Study ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes");
Figures [8](#S4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 4.3 Baselines ‣ 4 Experimental setup. ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")
and [15](#A4.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ D.6 Self-Reflection Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")).
For non-canonical artwork, where the final learned policy is utilized,
ArtMine still outperform baselines
(Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Abductive Process Discovery ‣ 5 A Case Study ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes");
Figure [16](#A4.F16 "Figure 16 ‣ D.6 Self-Reflection Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")),
indicating that it carries the process knowledge across artworks.

Rendering the underlying process remains more challenging than rendering
the final image. For non-canonical artworks, image generation is also
done stage-wise. Without conditioning on the prior stage, direct
stage-wise generation has no partial state to build from, so it renders
each stage’s prompt as a complete image. As a result, early stages
appear complete rather than as intermediate steps in the process. This
raises the final-stage fidelity score but does not expose the process’s
intermediate progression. Guided generation conditions each stage on the
previous image, preserving continuity across the sequence. But since
this conditioning is image-to-image rather than a fresh render only from
the prompt, early errors propagate and compound, causing the final
output to drift from the reference (Refer to Table
[2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Abductive Process Discovery ‣ 5 A Case Study ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")
and
Figures [7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4.1 Experimental details ‣ 4 Experimental setup. ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")
and [17](#A4.F17 "Figure 17 ‣ D.6 Self-Reflection Prompt ‣ Appendix D Prompt Templates ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes")).
Policy learning and transfer may have improved final artwork
reconstruction, but faithful process rendering is still difficult. This
leaves two open questions: how a generative system can learn to
represent the artistic process rather than only the appearance of
finished artworks, and whether intermediate artistic states such as
underdrawing, blocking-in, and glazing can be evaluated as meaningful
outputs rather than treated only as steps toward a final image.

## 6 Discussion and Limitations

Our work explores a process-centered perspective on computational
creativity by shifting attention from the generation of artistic
artifacts to the discovery and formalization of creative workflows.
Rather than treating artworks as isolated outputs, the proposed
framework models artistic production as a sequence of situated decisions
grounded in material practice, historical context, and stylistic
evolution. This framing aligns with broader directions in human-AI
co-creativity that emphasize interaction, interpretation, and reflective
collaboration over autonomous artifact generation. By maintaining
explicit links between inferred actions and supporting evidence, the
framework also moves toward more interpretable and auditable forms of
creative AI systems.

A central contribution of the work is the formulation of artistic
process inference as an abductive reasoning problem over heterogeneous
historical evidence. Unlike domains with formal verification signals,
artistic workflows are inherently underdetermined: multiple plausible
trajectories may explain the same completed work, and historical
documentation is often incomplete, contradictory, or unevenly preserved.
Consequently, the framework should not be understood as recovering
definitive historical truth, but as constructing evidence-grounded and
procedurally coherent hypotheses that support historical interpretation
and creative reasoning. In this sense, the system is intended to
complement, rather than replace, expert art-historical analysis.

The proposed framework also highlights the emerging role of research
agents as knowledge-synthesis systems for computational humanities and
creative domains. While recent agentic systems primarily focus on
factual retrieval or task execution, our approach uses iterative
evidence gathering, structured memory construction, and abductive
reasoning to support process-level inference. More broadly, this
suggests opportunities for combining large language models, historical
archives, and reasoning frameworks in domains where procedural knowledge
is implicit and distributed.

At the same time, the work has several important limitations. First, the
framework depends heavily on the availability and quality of historical
evidence. Artists with extensive archival documentation, technical
studies, or correspondence are substantially easier to model than
artists whose practices are sparsely documented. As a result, the system
may implicitly privilege historically preserved artistic traditions
while underrepresenting oral, collaborative, marginalized, or
non-Western creative practices where process documentation is limited or
differently structured.

Second, abductive inference in creative domains remains fundamentally
uncertain. The inferred workflows represent plausible interpretations
conditioned on available evidence and modeling assumptions rather than
verified historical reconstructions. Although the framework maintains
explicit evidence traceability and structured reasoning, these
mechanisms do not eliminate the epistemic ambiguity inherent in modeling
historical creative processes.

This work should be viewed as a preliminary proof-of-concept rather than
a definitive computational model of artistic creation. Our evaluation
remains exploratory, emphasizing interpretability, coherence, and
evidential grounding over objective correctness. Future work can extend
this direction through richer multimodal evidence, uncertainty-aware
abduction, interactive co-creative systems, and collaboration with art
historians, conservators, and artists. More broadly, we hope this
encourages process-centered approaches to computational creativity,
artistic reasoning, and human-AI co-creativity.

## Appendix A Related Work

### A.1 Research Agents, Personas, and Creative AI

Recent research-agent systems extend retrieval-augmented generation with
iterative planning, tool use, reflection, and web interaction ([Lewis et
al., 2020](#bib.bib11); [Yao et al., 2022](#bib.bib5); [Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib6); [Nakano et al., 2021](#bib.bib4)). These systems
demonstrate that language agents can gather and synthesize information
from heterogeneous online sources through multi-step reasoning and
interaction. Our work builds on this direction by using a Deep Research
agent to gather evidence from multiple sources, synthesize claims across
these sources, assign reliability tags to retrieved evidence, and
organize the resulting information into a structured evidence repository
for downstream abductive reasoning. Rather than treating retrieved
information as unstructured context for generation, the resulting
evidence is organized into structured representations that support
downstream reasoning about creative processes.

Role-conditioned and persona-conditioned language agents aim to maintain
behavioral or stylistic consistency during generation. Early work
represented personas through static textual profiles in dialogue systems
([Zhang et al., 2018b](#bib.bib13); [Mazaré et al., 2018](#bib.bib12)),
while more recent approaches study role-playing and
character-conditioned generation in large language models. ArtPeer
([Kumar et al.,](#bib.bib14) ) explores artist-centered persona
construction from art-historical sources, while CharacterGLM ([Zhou et
al., 2024](#bib.bib15)) studies character-consistent generation under
persona conditioning. In most of these systems, personas primarily
function as conditioning mechanisms for generating stylistically or
behaviorally consistent outputs. In contrast, our framework evaluates
discovered process trajectories through artwork-grounded policy
optimization, where rendered artwork are compared with reference
artworks and the resulting deviations drive self-reflection-based policy
updates.

Our work is also related to computational creativity and generative art
systems. Classical systems such as AARON ([Cohen, 1995](#bib.bib7)) and
The Painting Fool ([Colton, 2012](#bib.bib8)) generate artworks through
procedural rules and heuristic creative strategies. More recent
generative models such as DALL$`\cdot`$E 3 ([Betker et al.,
2023](#bib.bib16)), Stable Diffusion ([Rombach et al.,
2022](#bib.bib3)), and Jukebox ([Dhariwal et al., 2020](#bib.bib17))
learn distributions over artistic artifacts from large-scale multimodal
data. Agent-based simulations of social behavior and interaction ([Park
et al., 2023](#bib.bib18)) similarly model emergent behaviors through
multi-agent interaction. In contrast, our work focuses on discovering
historically grounded creative trajectories from documentary, archival,
technical, and art-historical evidence, and refining them through
artwork-grounded self-reflection rather than treating generation as a
one-shot artifact-production task.

### A.2 Abductive Reasoning and Process Inference

Abductive reasoning, commonly described as inference to the best
explanation, was introduced by Peirce and later formalized in AI as
reasoning over hypotheses that explain observations under background
knowledge ([Peirce, 1997](#bib.bib10); [Pople, 1973](#bib.bib19);
[Josephson and Josephson, 1996](#bib.bib44)). Subsequent work has
explored logic-based, probabilistic, and neural-symbolic formulations of
abduction ([Kakas et al., 1992](#bib.bib9); [Ng and Mooney,
1992](#bib.bib20); [Qiao et al., 2023](#bib.bib21)). More recently,
large language models have demonstrated abductive capabilities in
commonsense and explanatory reasoning tasks ([Bhagavatula et al.,
2019](#bib.bib22); [Weng et al., 2023](#bib.bib23)). However, these
approaches typically rely on unconstrained generation and often lack
explicit mechanisms for grounding hypotheses in structured external
evidence or comparing competing explanations under domain-specific
constraints.

Our framework treats artistic process reconstruction as an abductive
inference problem grounded in heterogeneous historical evidence. Artwork
features act as observations, documentary and conservation records
provide contextual knowledge, and reconstructed production steps form
candidate hypotheses. The reasoning process is guided by a structured
Peircean abductive framework that maintains explicit connections between
observations, inferred actions, and supporting evidence.

The work is also related to procedural and process-oriented modeling
systems such as Voyager ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib24)), ChemCrow
([Bran et al., 2023](#bib.bib25)), and BioPlanner ([O’Donoghue et al.,
2023](#bib.bib26)), which generate executable procedures from
unstructured inputs. These approaches often rely on external
environments or formal verification signals for evaluation. In contrast,
artistic process reconstruction rarely admits definitive correctness
criteria because historical workflows are only partially observable. Our
framework therefore evaluates reconstructed processes through
evidence-grounded plausibility assessments informed by artist-specific
and movement-specific context.

### A.3 Computational Art History and Process Discovery

Prior work in computational art history has focused primarily on
analyzing completed artistic artifacts through tasks such as attribution
([Elgammal et al., 2018](#bib.bib27); [Joshi et al., 2026](#bib.bib31);
[Van Noord et al., 2015](#bib.bib53); [Ji et al., 2021](#bib.bib54);
[Ugail et al., 2023](#bib.bib55)), classification ([Karayev et al.,
2013](#bib.bib28); [Dangeti et al., 2024](#bib.bib51); [Saleh and
Elgammal, 2015](#bib.bib52); [Strafforello et al., 2025](#bib.bib56);
[Limpijankit et al., 2026](#bib.bib57)), stylistic similarity ([Seguin
et al., 2016](#bib.bib29)), interpretability ([Gatys et al.,
2015](#bib.bib30); [Bau et al., 2019](#bib.bib32); [Schneider,
2026](#bib.bib58); [Bau et al., 2018](#bib.bib59)), and style transfer
([Zhu et al., 2017](#bib.bib33); [Karras et al., 2020](#bib.bib34); [He
et al., 2026](#bib.bib60); [Guo et al., 2026](#bib.bib61)). These
approaches have significantly advanced the understanding of visual
representations, stylistic structures, and semantic organization in
artworks, enabling large-scale analysis of artistic movements, painterly
styles, and cross-modal aesthetic relationships. More recently,
generative models have further expanded the scope of computational art
analysis by learning high-dimensional distributions over artistic
artifacts from large multimodal datasets. However, despite these
advances, most existing approaches remain artifact-centric: they analyze
completed works or synthesize stylistically plausible outputs without
explicitly modeling the procedural, historical, and contextual dynamics
underlying artistic production.

Our work instead focuses on artistic processes as the primary object of
inference. In contrast to tasks such as attribution or style transfer,
which operate on observable visual properties of final artworks,
artistic process discovery requires reasoning about latent creative
trajectories that are only partially reflected in the completed
artifact. These trajectories often involve iterative experimentation,
revisions, material constraints, environmental influences, and
interactions with broader artistic movements or social contexts. Such
information is rarely available in a single structured source and
instead exists in fragmented forms distributed across archival records,
correspondence, technical analyses, interviews, biographies,
conservation studies, preparatory sketches, and art-historical
scholarship.

Our work is additionally related to process discovery methods developed
in areas such as workflow mining and business process analysis ([Huser,
2012](#bib.bib35); [Leemans et al., 2013](#bib.bib36)), where latent
procedures are reconstructed from structured event logs and execution
traces. In these domains, process discovery typically assumes explicit
temporal records, well-defined state transitions, and relatively
objective notions of correctness. Artistic domains differ substantially
because creative workflows are inherently ambiguous, non-linear, and
historically underdetermined. Process traces are fragmented, selectively
preserved, and frequently mediated through interpretation rather than
direct observation. As a result, reconstructing artistic workflows
cannot rely on exact procedural recovery and instead requires reasoning
under uncertainty over heterogeneous evidence sources.

## Appendix B Populated Memory

This appendix presents the full memory $`M_{\text{evidence}}`$ produced
by the deep-research agent for Leonardo da Vinci’s _Mona Lisa_ and
Edvard Munch’s _The Scream_ , organized across the eleven typed
categories defined in
[Section 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Evidence Construction ‣ 3 Method ‣ ArtMine: Discovering and Formalizing Artistic Processes").
Each category is presented as a JSON document with evidence_type tags,
source citations, and conflict flags as specified by the schema.

### B.1 Mona Lisa

#### B.1.1 Metadata

```ltx_verbatim
{
  "metadata": {
    "title": {
      "primary": "Portrait of Lisa Gherardini, wife of Francesco del
                  Giocondo, known as La Joconde or Mona Lisa",
      "alternates": ["Mona Lisa", "La Joconde", "Monna Lisa",
                     "La Gioconda"],
      "evidence_type": "direct_evidence",
      "source": "Louvre Collections, INV 779"

trajectories are compactly shown using the first three and last three
stages. Across the non-canonical artworks—Horse and Cart by Georges
Seurat, Two Riders by a River by Edgar Degas, Cat and Canary by Will
Barnet, and A Walk at Dusk by Caspar David Friedrich; we observe
complementary failure modes. Direct generation completes the artwork too
early because each stage is rendered as a near-final image, whereas
guided generation better preserves stage-to-stage continuity but can
accumulate errors and drift in style over later stages.
